slot.brief: Ask why transition metal ions are coloured (d–d transition) and match a given ion with its colour.

stem: Transition metal ions in aqueous solution are coloured primarily due to \_\_\_\_\_\_, and the characteristic colour of $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_.

verdicts.working: Aqueous transition metal ions with partially filled d orbitals absorb visible light via d–d transitions (crystal field splitting). [Cu(H2O)6]2+ absorbs red/orange light and appears blue. Hence d–d transition; blue.

working:
The colour of transition metal ions in aqueous solution arises from the absorption of visible light that promotes an electron from a lower-energy $d$-orbital to a higher-energy $d$-orbital within the ligand-field split $d$-subshell; this phenomenon is termed a $d\text{--}d$ transition. The $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion has a $3d^9$ electronic configuration (one unpaired electron). In aqueous solution, it forms the hydrated complex $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, which absorbs light in the red-orange region and transmits the complementary colour, appearing distinctly blue.

draft.distractor_notes: Option A: Correctly identifies the $d\text{--}d$ transition mechanism but mistakes the colour of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ for green (which is typical of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ or $\text{Ni}^{2+}$). Option C: Correctly identifies the blue colour of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, but confuses the cause of colour with charge transfer (which is responsible for colour in $d^0$ oxoanions like $\text{MnO}_4^-$). Option D: Both the mechanism (charge transfer) and colour (green) are incorrect.
